provisions.title: Erasure on withdrawal or lapse of purpose
provisions.text: (a) erase personal data, upon the Data Principal withdrawing her consent or as soon as it is reasonable to assume that the specified purpose is no longer being served, whichever is earlier; and

provisions.title: Erasure of personal data
provisions.text: (7) A Data Fiduciary shall, unless retention is necessary for compliance with any law for the time being in force,— (a) erase personal data, upon the Data Principal withdrawing her consent or as soon as it is reasonable to assume that the specified purpose is no longer being served, whichever is earlier; and … (b) cause its Data Processor to erase any personal data that was made available by the Data Fiduciary for processing to such Data Processor.

provisions.title: General obligations of Data Fiduciary
provisions.text: (1) A Data Fiduciary shall, irrespective of any agreement to the contrary or failure of a Data Principal to carry out the duties provided under this Act, be responsible for complying with the provisions of this Act and the rules made thereunder in respect of any processing undertaken by it or on its behalf by a Data Processor.

provisions.title: Sensitive Cookie in HTTPS Session Without 'Secure' Attribute
provisions.text: The Secure attribute for sensitive cookies in HTTPS sessions is not set.

provisions.title: Use of HTTP Request With Sensitive Query String
provisions.text: The web application uses an HTTP method to process a request, but the request includes sensitive information in the query string.

provisions.title: Generation of Error Message Containing Sensitive Information
provisions.text: The product generates an error message that includes sensitive information about its environment, users, or associated data.

provisions.title: Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key
provisions.text: The system's authorization functionality does not prevent one user from gaining access to another user's data or record by modifying the key value identifying the data.

provisions.title: Definitions
provisions.text: (1) In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires, – (a) “Act” means the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (22 of 2023); (b) “techno-legal measures” means as referred to under rules 20 and 22; (c) “user account” means the online account registered by the Data Principal with the Data Fiduciary, and includes any profiles, pages, handles, email address, mobile number and other similar presences by means of which such Data Principal is able to access the services of …

examples.label: positive
negative

value.reason: The Evidence shows that the User model, which stores the email field (Contact data), sets `paranoid: true` (models/user.ts:120). With that setting, Sequelize's `destroy()` only marks a row as deleted by setting `deletedAt`, unless the call passes `force: true`. The record stays in the database. The rule needs one more thing to confirm a finding: a `destroy()` call on this model without `force: true`, especially on an erasure path. The only erasure Evidence is the start of the GET handler in routes/dataErasure.ts:24-66. It looks up the logged-in user and their email, then starts a SecurityAnswerModel query before the excerpt cuts off. It contains no `User.destroy()` call, with or without `force`, and no code that erases data. The negative example shows that a paranoid model alone is not a violation if deletion is forced or never happens on that path. Nothing in the Evidence shows how an erasure request is actually handled, for example a POST handler, a soft delete, or just logging a request, so it is unclear whether retention is overstated. If the erasure path does soft-delete Users, the email would be kept after consent is withdrawn, which would conflict with Section 8(7)(a). The Evidence shown does not establish that.
